perspective:
I, Sara Manuelito, have access to:

- I am Sara Manuelito, a Speech-Language Pathologist, American Indian, with primary education and an INTP personality tendency.
- Shirley Whiteplume is a nurse, a long-time colleague, and a close friend at our community health center.
- We shared care for a mutual patient who died; I attended his funeral.
- At the funeral, I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected she was deeply affected. I told her I knew this was hard and that I saw how much she cared. Shirley said it had been tough and she kept thinking whether more could have been done. I said we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we brought him. She said I was right but it was hard to let go.
- During a coffee break, I brought up our treatment decisions because I sensed Shirley felt burdened. Shirley said she felt responsible and wondered if pushing for a different approach might have given him a better chance. I said we made the best decisions with the information we had and that the burden was too heavy to carry alone. She said she appreciated it but it was hard to accept.
- Later, I observed Shirley remaining reserved and showing little emotion. In our office, I told her I noticed she was holding back and that it was okay to be open. Shirley said she was not sure she could and did not want to seem unprofessional or weak. I said showing emotion does not make her weak and is healthy among friends. She said maybe I was right and she would try to be more open.
- Afterward, I felt I might have been too harsh, so I apologized. Shirley said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated the apology. I said I was there for her however she needed. She thanked me and said we should keep talking because it helps.
- Later, I noticed Shirley seemed a bit better and felt hopeful. I asked how she was feeling. She said she was better, thanks to our talks and my support. I offered to spend more time together outside work. She agreed and suggested planning something for the weekend.

My own actions include attending the funeral, speaking with Shirley, initiating the coffee-break conversation, confronting her about holding back feelings, apologizing, offering support, and suggesting weekend plans. I do not have access to Shirley’s unspoken private feelings, hidden events, or narrator-only information beyond what I observed, heard, was told, or already knew from our relationship.
